lead: A design pattern is a named, reusable answer to a design problem that keeps returning. It is not code to copy. It is a small arrangement of roles and responsibilities that you adapt to your own classes. Patterns exist because designers kept meeting the same problems: one change must reach many screens, an old API must fit a new app, and a messy subsystem must look simple. A pattern is worth using only when its cost — extra classes, indirection, learning time — is smaller than the problem it removes. Four patterns common in web and Android apps follow.
prereq: You need: 3.2 for abstraction and information hiding, and 3.3 for where MVC usually appears.

sections.h3: Why patterns exist and the three families

blocks.text: A pattern has a name, a problem, a solution and consequences. The name lets a team say 'use an observer here' and share a design idea in three words. The consequences are the costs you accept. The Gang of Four (GoF) grouped patterns into three families.

blocks.text: Creational patterns hide construction choices. Structural patterns shape composition. Behavioural patterns organise communication. The four patterns below are not the whole catalog; they are the ones that appear most in design questions.

Use a pattern when the problem is recurring and the pattern's vocabulary helps the team. Do not force a pattern into a one-off class. Patterns are not frameworks; a library is code you call, a framework is code that calls your code (inversion of control), and a pattern is a design you apply.

MVC splits an interactive application into three roles. The model holds data and business rules. The view draws the data. The controller receives user input, updates the model, and chooses a view. A button press goes to the controller, not straight to the model. The model does not know which views show it, so you can change the screen without changing the rules. Cost: more classes and a flow that jumps between three places, so a small screen may not need MVC. Some syllabi call MVC an architectural pattern because it organises the whole application, not one class.

Observer defines a one-to-many dependency. A subject holds a list of observers. Each observer registers by calling subject.attach(this); the subject keeps the observer in its list. When state changes, the subject calls notify() on every observer. In push, notify carries the new state as an argument. In pull, notify only says 'changed'; each observer calls getState() to fetch what it needs. Pull is flexible but costs extra calls. Push sends data that some observers may ignore. Cost: observers must be attached and detached correctly; a forgotten observer receives updates forever and can leak memory. Use it for stock feeds, news alerts, GUI event listeners and model-to-view updates.

Adapter converts the interface of one class into the interface a client already expects. The client calls its own method name; the adapter translates to the old method. In an object adapter, the adapter holds one instance of the old class and delegates. In a class adapter, the adapter inherits from the old class; this needs multiple inheritance, so Java and C# cannot do it in the plain way. Use an adapter when an old bank API has debitAcct(String account, int paise) but your app has pay(String account, double rupees). The adapter multiplies rupees by 100, converts to int, and calls debitAcct. Cost: one more object and a place where conversion bugs hide; rounding must be decided.

Facade gives one simple interface to a set of subsystems. A DashboardFacade may have loadSalesPanel(), loadStockPanel() and loadAlertsPanel(); each hides calls to many classes. A facade does not add new function. It only makes the same function easier to call. It reduces coupling for the client, but the subsystems still exist and can be used directly. Cost: if the facade becomes the only door, a missing method forces a change in the facade. Use it for dashboards, startup sequences and wrapping a library with many setup steps. Do not call it an adapter: an adapter changes one interface; a facade simplifies many. UI design patterns such as dashboard, wizard and breadcrumb are reusable screen layouts, not GoF patterns.

examples.question: Question (6 marks). Pick the best pattern for each case and justify with the numbers. (a) A stock-price feed has 500 registered clients and must push every price change to all of them; the feed changes 20 times per second. Compare with polling every 100 ms. (b) A new app must call an old bank API whose method is debitAcct(String account, int paise). The app works in rupees, for example ₹250.75. (c) A dashboard screen has 30 subsystems behind it and the screen code should call one method per panel.
steps: (a) Pattern: observer. Subject = price feed, observers = 500 clients. Push messages per second = 20 × 500 = 10,000.

Polling: 100 ms = 0.1 s, so each client polls 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10 times per second. For 500 clients, requests per second = 10 × 500 = 5,000. Push sends 10,000 update messages/s; polling sends 5,000 requests/s even when the price does not change.
(b) Pattern: adapter. Convert ₹250.75 to paise: 250.75 × 100 = 25,075 paise. The adapter calls debitAcct(account, 25075).
(c) Pattern: facade. One DashboardFacade with methods such as loadSalesPanel() hides the 30 subsystems. It adds no new function.
examples.check:
changes_per_sec = 20
clients = 500
push = changes_per_sec * clients
print(push)
poll_interval_s = 100 / 1000
polls_per_s = 1 / poll_interval_s
poll = polls_per_s * clients
print(int(poll))
rupees = 250.75
paise = round(rupees * 100)
print(paise)

traps: Adapter versus facade: an adapter changes one interface into the interface the client expects; a facade puts one simpler interface over many classes. 'Wraps many classes to make them easy' is facade.
MVC model is not the database. The model is data plus business rules; a database is one way to store it.
Observer notify() is not always the same as update(). In pull, notify only signals; getState() fetches the state.
Class adapter needs multiple inheritance. Java and C# use object adapters; claiming class adapter in Java is an error.
A facade adds no new business function. If it adds new behaviour, it is more than a facade.

quiz.q: Name the three GoF pattern families and give one pattern from each other than MVC, observer, adapter and facade.
quiz.a: Creational: Singleton. Structural: Proxy. Behavioural: Strategy.

quiz.q: In MVC, why does the view not read user input directly?
quiz.a: The controller receives input, updates the model and chooses the view. This keeps the view replaceable and keeps business rules out of screen code.

quiz.q: A feed has 50 changes per second and 200 clients. How many update messages per second does observer push send? If clients polled every 200 ms instead, how many requests per second?
quiz.a: Push: 50 × 200 = 10,000 messages/s. Polling: 200 ms = 0.2 s, so 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5 polls/s per client; 5 × 200 = 1,000 requests/s.

quiz.q: A team wraps 12 payment gateways behind one PaymentFacade with pay(). Is this adapter or facade? Why?
quiz.a: Facade. One simple interface hides many subsystem classes. An adapter would convert one gateway's interface into the interface the client already expects.

quiz.q: An adapter receives ₹199.99 and must pass paise as int. What value does it pass?
quiz.a: It passes 19,999 paise. With rupees = 199.99, paise = (int) Math.round(rupees * 100) gives 19,999. A plain cast (int)(rupees * 100) gives 19,998 because of floating-point error, so round explicitly or use BigDecimal.

quiz.q: What does observer pull cost compared with push?
quiz.a: Pull adds one getState call per observer per change. Push sends the payload in notify but may send data that some observers ignore.

quiz.q: Why is a facade not a substitute for fixing a bad subsystem design?
quiz.a: A facade hides complexity but does not remove it. Clients through the facade are simpler, but direct users and maintenance still face the subsystems; the facade can grow into a god class.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, MVC has grown into MVVM and MVP on Android and web front ends, and observer is built into event buses, React state and Rx streams. An adapter example is Java's InputStreamReader, an object adapter over a byte stream. A facade example is a small class that wraps a multi-step JDBC setup (load driver, open connection, prepare statement) behind one method. Spring's JdbcTemplate is primarily an example of Template Method, not facade. Search for 'Model-View-ViewModel', 'reactive streams' and 'hexagonal architecture ports and adapters' to see where these ideas go. Pattern catalogs now include cloud patterns such as circuit breaker and sidecar.
